newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish market recovery seen hitting top soon.
newsitem.headline: Spanish market recovery seen hitting top soon.

text.p: Spain's financial markets revived on Monday, buoyed by renewed expectations of lower interest rates and more positive sentiment on prospects for the launch of the single euro currency, analysts said.
This followed progress at a weekend meeting of European Union finance ministers (Ecofin) in the Netherlands and news on Spain's stability plan, analysts said.
But dealers remained cautious and analysts said it would be difficult to top current levels with further U.S. rate increases expected, which would hang over European markets.
"It's a bit weird. We came back from holiday and everybody was buying assets that previously they did not want to touch," said Emilio Sainz, a dealer at Natwest in Madrid.
"The market is looking better but we've had no more than a bout of short-covering... further falls are ahead," Sainz added.
At midday, the peseta was trading around 84.42/45 against the mark, compared with levels near to 85 at the beginning of March.

The 10-year cash yield spread over German Bunds was trading at 100 basis points versus 140 in early March, while the Ibex-35 index of leading shares had climbed 83.91 points, of 1.57 percent, to 5,417.59.
Spain pledged earlier on Monday to reduce its public deficit to 1.6 percent of gross domestic product in 2000 from a planned 3.0 percent in 1997.

Dealers said the plan presented to ensure Spain's fiscal stability into the next century had helped buoy markets, although the effect had not been great and analysts were not optimistic about further gains.
"The room for further falls in long-term yields below the seven percent level is little," said Felix Gonzalez Martin, chief economist at Beta Capital.

"Stocks benefited from Wall Street's positive close on Friday and from the Ecofin," said Philippe Sardet chief dealer at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid. But he expected the market to remain highly volatile in the short run.
"The market's volatility is still very high and it's impossible to rule out a fall tomorrow," Sardet added.
Ten-year yields had retreated to 7.00 percent from 7.30 percent in early March, while two-year yields were down to around 5.75 percent from highs at 6.10 percent.

"We have both the short and the long end well supported for two different reasons -- renewed expectations of a rate cut here in Spain and Euro-optimism," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
Spain's February producer price data boosted market optimism for the March consumer price index (CPI) statistics, coming in lower than expected at 0.5 percent year-on-year.
Analysts expect March CPI to rise at around 2.3/2.4 percent year-on-year versus 2.5 percent in February.
"This will give the Bank of Spain room to cut its key money market rate at least one more time," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.
"Before, there was the feeling peripheral markets would have to put further rate cuts on hold. But in the last 10 days we changed our forecasts," said Giordano.
March CPI is scheduled to be released on Friday and the Bank of Spain's repurchase tender will be on April 15.
A shift in investment back to southern European currencies such as the lira or the peseta was probably due to the covering of previous short positions, dealers said.

The 10-year spread over Bunds, a measure of market sentiment on European economic and monetary union (EMU), is higher than its minimum of 83 basis points hit in January, although political determination to see the single European currency launched in 1999 appears as solid as ever.
"The decision of (German Chancellor Helmut) Kohl, one of EMU's stronger supporters, to stand for re-election in 1998 and the Ecofin meeting brought about a shift in the "Euromood"," said Lumholdt.
But Spain's markets will remain wary of any anti-EMU remarks and of U.S. market developments, analysts said.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
